title: MATH2010 Module 05: Characterization of Invertible Matrices and Matrix Factorizations

questions.q: Let A be an n×n matrix. Which statements are equivalent to “A is invertible”?
choices: A is row equivalent to the n×n identity matrix
The columns of A form a linearly independent set
Ax = 0 has at least one solution
Ax = b is consistent for every b in ℝⁿ
Ax = b is consistent for at least one b in ℝⁿ
The transformation x ↦ Ax maps ℝⁿ onto ℝⁿ
A has at least one pivot column
questions.explain: Those five are statements of the Invertible Matrix Theorem. The other three hold for many non-invertible matrices: x = 0 always solves Ax = 0, b = 0 always gives a consistent system, and any nonzero matrix has a pivot column.

questions.q: For an n×n matrix A, the statements “the columns of A span ℝⁿ” and “x ↦ Ax is one-to-one” are either both true or both false.
questions.explain: Both are statements of the IMT, so for a square matrix they are true together or false together. For non-square matrices this equivalence fails.

questions.q: A is a 4×4 matrix and Ax = 0 has only the trivial solution. Which of these must be true?
choices: The columns of A span ℝ⁴
A has a row of zeros
Ax = b is inconsistent for some b in ℝ⁴
questions.explain: “Only the trivial solution” is an IMT statement, so A is invertible and every other IMT statement holds, including that the columns span ℝ⁴. Each of the other choices would make A non-invertible.

questions.q: If A is n×n and there is an n×n matrix C with CA = I, then Aᵀ is invertible.
questions.explain: Having a matrix C with CA = I is an IMT statement, so A is invertible. Aᵀ being invertible is another IMT statement, so it holds too.

questions.q: A is 5×5 and the transformation x ↦ Ax is not onto ℝ⁵. Which of these must be true?
choices: A has a column of zeros
Two columns of A are equal
Ax = b is inconsistent for every nonzero b
questions.explain: “Onto” is an IMT statement. When it fails, they all fail, including “Ax = 0 has only the trivial solution”. A zero column or two equal columns would each make A non-invertible, but neither is forced. The failure only guarantees that SOME b gives an inconsistent system, not every nonzero b.

questions.q: For a square matrix A, if the rows of A are linearly independent, then A is invertible.
questions.explain: The rows of A are the columns of Aᵀ. Independent columns make Aᵀ invertible by the IMT, and Aᵀ is invertible exactly when A is.

questions.q: If an n×n matrix has a pivot in every column, why is Ax = b consistent for every b?
choices: n pivots in n rows means every row has a pivot, so an echelon form of [A | b] can never contain a row [0 ⋯ 0 | nonzero]
A pivot in every column means there are no free variables
Every system Ax = b is consistent when b = 0
A pivot in every column means A equals its transpose
questions.explain: A pivot in every column on its own gives uniqueness (no free variables), not existence. Counting gives existence: n pivots in an n×n matrix put a pivot in every row too. That is why uniqueness and existence come together for square matrices.

questions.q: Fill in the blank (one word): for any given n×n matrix, the statements of the Invertible Matrix Theorem are either all true or all ____.
questions.explain: “Equivalent” means there is no mixed case. Showing any one statement is true proves all of them, and showing any one is false disproves all of them.

questions.q: A is 3×3 and its columns are linearly dependent. Which of the IMT statements hold for A?
choices: All of them except the linear-independence statement
It depends on the entries of A
questions.explain: The linear-independence statement is false, and the IMT statements are all true or all false, so every one of them is false. In particular Aᵀ is not invertible either.

questions.category: IMT: applying it to a matrix
questions.q: Which argument correctly applies the IMT to the matrix A with rows (1, 3, 4), (0, 9, −12), (0, 0, 19)?
choices: A is already in echelon form with pivots 1, 9, 19, so every column is a pivot column and A is invertible
A has zeros below the diagonal, so its columns are linearly dependent and A is not invertible
A has a negative entry, so it is not row equivalent to I
The IMT cannot be applied until A⁻¹ has been computed
questions.explain: Each nonzero row starts further right than the one above, so A is in echelon form with pivots in positions (1,1), (2,2), (3,3). A pivot in every column is an IMT statement, so A is invertible. Zeros below the diagonal and negative entries say nothing against invertibility.

questions.category: IMT: applying it to a matrix
questions.q: The matrix with rows (1, 0, 4), (4, 0, 0), (−2, 0, 12) is invertible.
questions.explain: Its second column is the zero vector, so 0·a₁ + 1·a₂ + 0·a₃ = 0 is a nontrivial dependence relation. The columns are linearly dependent, so by the IMT the matrix is not invertible.

questions.category: IMT: applying it to a matrix
questions.q: Let A have rows (1, 0, 4), (4, 0, 0), (−2, 0, 12). Which vector is a nontrivial solution of Ax = 0?
questions.explain: Ax = x₁(column 1) + x₂(column 2) + x₃(column 3). Column 2 is zero, so x = (0, 1, 0) gives 0. The other vectors give (1, 4, −2), (4, 0, 12), and (5, 4, 10).

questions.category: IMT: applying it to a matrix
questions.q: A has rows (1, 0, 0), (−3, 3, 0), (2, 7, 12). Which observation, combined with the IMT, shows that A is invertible?
choices: Aᵀ has rows (1, −3, 2), (0, 3, 7), (0, 0, 12). It is in echelon form with a pivot in every column, so Aᵀ is invertible, and therefore so is A
A is lower triangular, so it is already in echelon form with three pivots
Entry (1, 2) of A is 0, so the columns of A are linearly independent
The first row of A has two zeros, so A is row equivalent to I
questions.explain: A itself is not in echelon form, because there are nonzero entries below the (1,1) pivot. Its transpose is upper triangular and in echelon form with pivots 1, 3, 12. Row reducing A directly also works: R2 + 3R1, R3 − 2R1, then R3 − (7/3)R2 leaves pivots 1, 3, 12.

questions.category: IMT: applying it to a matrix
questions.q: The lower triangular matrix with rows (1, 0, 0), (−3, 3, 0), (2, 7, 12) is already in echelon form.
questions.explain: Echelon form needs zeros below each leading entry. Here −3 and 2 sit below the leading 1 in column 1. A lower triangular matrix is in echelon form only if its entries below the diagonal are already 0. Upper triangular matrices with nonzero diagonals are the ones that are already in echelon form.

questions.category: IMT: applying it to a matrix
questions.q: Is the matrix with rows (2, 4), (1, 2) invertible?
choices: No: column 2 is 2 times column 1, so the columns are linearly dependent
Yes: it has no zero row
questions.explain: The columns are (2, 1) and (4, 2) = 2(2, 1), so they are dependent, and by the IMT the matrix is not invertible. Nonzero columns and the lack of a zero row are not enough. Whether a matrix is triangular says nothing about invertibility.

questions.category: IMT: applying it to a matrix
questions.q: Which of these 3×3 matrices are NOT invertible?
questions.explain: Rows (1, 2, 3), (0, 0, 5), (0, 0, 7): column 2 = 2 × column 1, so the columns are dependent (it is triangular with a 0 on the diagonal). Rows (1, 2, 3), (2, 4, 6), (0, 1, 1): row 2 = 2 × row 1, so Aᵀ has dependent columns. The matrix with a zero row: Aᵀ has a zero column. The lower triangular matrix with diagonal 3, −1, 4 and the diagonal matrix with diagonal 2, 5, −1 have nonzero diagonal entries, so they are invertible.

questions.category: IMT: applying it to a matrix
questions.q: For which value of k is the matrix with rows (1, 2), (3, k) NOT invertible?
questions.explain: R2 − 3R1 turns row 2 into (0, k − 6). Column 2 is a pivot column exactly when k − 6 ≠ 0. At k = 6 it has no pivot, so by the IMT the matrix is not invertible. Indeed, column 2 is then 2 × column 1.

questions.category: IMT: applying it to a matrix
questions.q: The matrix with rows (2, 5, −1), (0, h, 3), (0, 0, 4) is invertible for every value of h except one. What is that value?
questions.explain: For h ≠ 0 the matrix is in echelon form with pivots 2, h, 4, so every column is a pivot column. For h = 0, row 2 becomes (0, 0, 3), and R3 − (4/3)R2 makes row 3 zero. Only two pivots remain and column 2 is not a pivot column.

questions.category: IMT: applying it to a matrix
questions.q: A is 3×3 and its third column equals the sum of its first two columns. Which conclusion is correct?
choices: Ax = b is inconsistent for at least one b in ℝ³
Ax = 0 has only the trivial solution
questions.explain: a₁ + a₂ − a₃ = 0 is a nontrivial dependence relation (x = (1, 1, −1) solves Ax = 0), so A is not invertible. Every IMT statement then fails, including “Ax = b is consistent for each b”, so some b gives an inconsistent system.

questions.q: A 3×2 matrix whose columns are linearly independent is invertible.
questions.explain: Only square matrices can be invertible, and the IMT applies only to n×n matrices. Independent columns do not make a non-square matrix invertible.

questions.q: If x = 0 is a solution of Ax = 0, then the square matrix A is invertible.
questions.explain: x = 0 solves every homogeneous system. The IMT statement is that x = 0 is the ONLY solution.

questions.q: For a 2×3 matrix A, the transformation x ↦ Ax is one-to-one if and only if it is onto.
questions.explain: That equivalence comes from the IMT, which requires a square matrix. For example, the matrix with rows (1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0) maps ℝ³ onto ℝ², but it is not one-to-one, because both (0, 0, 1) and 0 map to 0.

questions.q: A student looks at A with rows (0, 1), (1, 0), sees a 0 in position (1, 1), and concludes that column 1 is not a pivot column, so A is not invertible. What is wrong?
choices: Pivot columns must be read from an echelon form. Swapping the rows gives I, so A is invertible
Nothing. A 0 in position (1, 1) always means A is not invertible
The student should have looked at position (2, 2) instead
Pivot columns are only defined for triangular matrices
questions.explain: You can't read pivot positions off A unless A is already in echelon form. Interchanging the two rows gives the identity, which has a pivot in every column, so A is invertible.

questions.q: Let A be n×n with n ≥ 2. If Ax = b is consistent for b = 0 and also for b = e₁, then A is invertible.
questions.explain: The IMT statement requires consistency for EACH b in ℝⁿ. For example, A with rows (1, 0), (0, 0) gives consistent systems for b = 0 and b = (1, 0), but not for b = (0, 1).

questions.q: Which of these matrices could be invertible?
choices: A 3×3 matrix whose columns span ℝ³
A 2×3 matrix whose columns span ℝ²
A 3×2 matrix with linearly independent columns
A 4×3 matrix with three pivot columns
questions.explain: Invertibility is only defined for square matrices, so the non-square options are out no matter what else is true. A 3×3 matrix whose columns span ℝ³ is invertible by the IMT.

questions.q: A square matrix with two identical rows can still be invertible.
questions.explain: Identical rows are linearly dependent, so Aᵀ has dependent columns and is not invertible. By the IMT, A is not invertible either.

questions.q: If A and D are 4×4 matrices and AD = I, then DA = I.
questions.explain: By the Corollary, AD = I with square matrices makes A invertible with A⁻¹ = D, so DA = A⁻¹A = I.

questions.q: A and B are n×n matrices with AB = I. Which statement is NOT necessarily true?
questions.explain: The Corollary gives A⁻¹ = B and B⁻¹ = A, so BA = I. A is invertible, so Aᵀ is too. A and B are inverses of each other, not equal. For example, A with rows (2, 0), (0, 1) and B with rows (1/2, 0), (0, 1).

questions.q: If A is 1×2, B is 2×1, and AB = I₁, then BA must equal I₂.
questions.explain: The Corollary requires square matrices. For example, A = [1 0] and B = the column (1, 0) give AB = [1] = I₁, but BA has rows (1, 0), (0, 0), which is not I₂.

questions.q: A and B are 3×3 matrices. What is the least you must check to confirm that B = A⁻¹?
choices: That AB = I (one product is enough)
That both AB = I and BA = I
That A and B have the same pivot columns
questions.explain: For square matrices, the Corollary says AB = I already gives A⁻¹ = B and B⁻¹ = A. The product BA = I then follows automatically.

questions.q: A has rows (2, 1), (5, 3) and B has rows (3, −1), (−5, 2). You compute AB and get I. What is A⁻¹?
choices: It cannot be determined without also computing BA
questions.explain: A and B are both 2×2 and AB = I, so by the Corollary A⁻¹ = B. You don't need to compute BA separately.

questions.q: If A and B are n×n and AB = I, then Ax = b has a solution for every b in ℝⁿ.
questions.explain: AB = I makes A invertible (the right-inverse statement of the IMT), and consistency for every b is another IMT statement. Concretely, x = Bb works: A(Bb) = (AB)b = b.

questions.q: A is 3×3 and Ax = 0 has a nontrivial solution. Is there a 3×3 matrix D with AD = I?
choices: No. AD = I would make A invertible, but a nontrivial solution of Ax = 0 means A is not invertible
Yes, but only if A is triangular
Only if A has a zero column
questions.explain: Having a matrix D with AD = I and having only the trivial solution of Ax = 0 are both IMT statements. The second is false, so the first is false too.

questions.q: A square matrix A = [a_ij] is lower triangular when:
questions.explain: j > i means the column index is larger than the row index, so the position is above the main diagonal. Lower triangular means those entries are zero. Entries on and below the diagonal can be anything, including 0.

questions.q: A square matrix A = [a_ij] is upper triangular when:
questions.explain: j < i means the column index is smaller than the row index, so the position is below the main diagonal. Upper triangular means everything below the diagonal is 0.

questions.q: Classify the matrix with rows (0, 0), (5, 0). It is:
questions.explain: The only entry above the diagonal, entry (1, 2), is 0, so the matrix is lower triangular and therefore triangular. Entry (2, 1) = 5 is below the diagonal and nonzero, so the matrix is neither upper triangular nor diagonal.

questions.q: Classify the matrix with rows (1, 0), (0, 0). It is:
questions.explain: Every off-diagonal entry is 0, so the matrix is diagonal, which means it is both lower and upper triangular (and so triangular). A 0 on the diagonal is allowed.

questions.q: A diagonal matrix must have all of its diagonal entries nonzero.
questions.explain: The definition only requires every entry off the main diagonal to be 0. Diagonal entries can be anything, including 0.

questions.q: The n×n zero matrix is a diagonal matrix.
questions.explain: All of its off-diagonal entries are 0, so it is both lower and upper triangular, which is the definition of diagonal.

questions.q: Every diagonal matrix is upper triangular.
questions.explain: A diagonal matrix is defined as one that is both lower AND upper triangular.

questions.q: A is a 4×4 lower triangular matrix. Which entry must be 0?
questions.explain: Lower triangular forces a_ij = 0 when j > i. For a_23, j = 3 > i = 2. The other three entries have j ≤ i and can be anything.

questions.q: How many entries of a 4×4 upper triangular matrix are required to be 0?
questions.explain: The entries with j < i must be 0: 1 in row 2, 2 in row 3, and 3 in row 4, for a total of 6.

questions.q: A triangular matrix with a 0 somewhere on its main diagonal is not invertible.
questions.explain: Take upper triangular A and let column k hold the first diagonal 0. Columns 1 through k have zeros below row k − 1, so at most k − 1 of them can contain pivots. Some column is therefore not a pivot column, and by the IMT A is not invertible. For lower triangular A, apply the same argument to Aᵀ.

questions.q: As defined in this section, the terms lower triangular, upper triangular, and diagonal apply only to square matrices.
questions.explain: Each definition starts with a square matrix A = [a_ij] of size n×n. This is why, for a non-square A, the U in A = LU is described as an echelon form of A, not as upper triangular.

questions.q: A is 5×3 and A = LU is an LU factorization. What are the sizes of L and U?
questions.explain: L is square, with size equal to the number of rows of A (m×m). U is an echelon form of A, so it is the same size as A (m×n).

questions.q: A is 3×5 and A = LU is an LU factorization. What are the sizes of L and U?
questions.explain: L is m×m, where m = 3 is the number of rows of A. U has the same size as A, 3×5.

questions.q: In an LU factorization of an m×n matrix A, which properties must L have?
choices: L has 1's on its main diagonal
L is the same size as A
Every entry of L below the main diagonal is nonzero
questions.explain: L is unit lower triangular, and it is square with size equal to the number of rows of A. It matches the size of A only when A is square. The entries below the diagonal are multipliers and can be 0. For example, entry (4, 2) of L in the 5×3 example is 0.

questions.q: In an LU factorization, U must be the reduced echelon form of A.
questions.explain: U only needs to be AN echelon form of A. Its pivots don't have to be 1, and the entries above the pivots don't have to be 0.

questions.q: If A is square and A = LU is an LU factorization, then U is upper triangular.
questions.explain: An echelon form of a square matrix has only zeros below the main diagonal, so it is upper triangular.

questions.q: The sufficient condition for an LU factorization limits the row operations you may use while reducing A to echelon form. Which operations does it allow?
choices: Adding a multiple of a row to a row below it
Multiplying a row by a nonzero constant
Adding a multiple of a row to a row above it
questions.explain: If A can be reduced to echelon form using only replacements that add a multiple of one row to a row BELOW it, then A has an LU factorization. Swaps, scaling, and upward replacements are not part of that condition.

questions.q: Which matrix CANNOT be reduced to echelon form using only downward row replacements?
questions.explain: With a 0 in position (1, 1) and a nonzero entry below it, a row swap is the only way to get a pivot at the top of column 1. Rows (2, 1), (6, 8) only need R2 − 3R1, and the other two matrices are already in echelon form.

questions.q: The matrix with rows (0, 1), (1, 1) has an LU factorization.
questions.explain: Suppose L has rows (1, 0), (a, 1) and U has rows (p, q), (0, r). Then LU has rows (p, q), (ap, aq + r). Matching entry (1, 1) forces p = 0, which makes entry (2, 1) equal to ap = 0. But that entry of A is 1, so no such L and U exist.

questions.q: Every m×n matrix has an LU factorization.
questions.explain: Only SOME matrices can be factored as A = LU. The matrix with rows (0, 1), (1, 1) is a counterexample.

questions.q: When finding U, why don't you scale rows so that each pivot is 1?
choices: U only has to be an echelon form, and scaling is not a downward row replacement, so it would break the structure A = LU with 1's on the diagonal of L
Scaling a row changes the solution set of Ax = 0
The pivots of U are required to be greater than 1
Scaling is allowed, but only on the last row
questions.explain: The pivots of U can be any nonzero numbers, such as 2 and 2 in the 5×3 example. Scaling doesn't change solution sets. The problem is that the factor recording the steps would no longer be unit lower triangular.

questions.category: LU factorization: computing L and U
questions.q: Which is an LU factorization of A with rows (2, 1), (6, 8)?
questions.explain: R2 ← R2 − 3R1 gives (0, 5), so U has rows (2, 1), (0, 5), and the multiplier 3 goes in entry (2, 1) of L. Check: row 2 of LU is 3(2, 1) + (0, 5) = (6, 8). The −3 version makes the sign error, the U with a pivot of 1 needed scaling, which isn't allowed, and the last L is upper triangular.

questions.category: LU factorization: computing L and U
questions.q: While reducing A to U, you perform R3 ← R3 + 4R1. What number goes in entry (3, 1) of L?
questions.explain: Write the step as R3 ← R3 − (−4)R1. The multiplier being subtracted is −4, so entry (3, 1) of L is −4. L records the step that undoes the operation.

questions.category: LU factorization: computing L and U
questions.q: While reducing A to U, you perform R2 ← R2 − 5R1. What number goes in entry (2, 1) of L?
questions.explain: For a step R_i ← R_i − m·R_j, entry (i, j) of L is m. Here m = 5.

questions.category: LU factorization: computing L and U
questions.q: A is the 5×3 matrix with rows (2, −3, 4), (−4, 8, −7), (6, −5, 14), (−6, 9, −12), (8, −6, 19). What is the first column of L in its LU factorization?
questions.explain: Divide the first pivot column by the pivot 2: (2, −4, 6, −6, 8)/2 = (1, −2, 3, −3, 4). The second choice forgets to divide, the third has the signs flipped, and L is 5×5, so its columns have 5 entries.

questions.category: LU factorization: computing L and U
questions.q: For the same 5×3 matrix, after the first pivot step the rows are (2, −3, 4), (0, 2, 1), (0, 4, 2), (0, 0, 0), (0, 6, 3). What is entry (5, 2) of L?
questions.explain: The second pivot is 2, and the entry below it in row 5 is 6, so the multiplier is 6/2 = 3 (R5 ← R5 − 3R2).

questions.category: LU factorization: computing L and U
questions.q: A is the 5×3 matrix with rows (2, −3, 4), (−4, 8, −7), (6, −5, 14), (−6, 9, −12), (8, −6, 19). How many pivots does U have in its LU factorization?
questions.explain: After the second pivot step, rows 3 to 5 are all zero, so U has rows (2, −3, 4), (0, 2, 1), and three zero rows. Column 3 is not a pivot column. That is fine, because U only needs to be an echelon form.

questions.category: LU factorization: computing L and U
questions.q: In the LU factorization of the 5×3 matrix with rows (2, −3, 4), (−4, 8, −7), (6, −5, 14), (−6, 9, −12), (8, −6, 19), columns 3, 4, and 5 of L can be taken from the 5×5 identity matrix.
questions.explain: U has only two pivots. Once you run out of pivots, the remaining columns of L are filled with the matching columns of I. Rows 3 to 5 of U are zero, so those columns of L don't affect the product LU.

questions.category: LU factorization: computing L and U
questions.explain: After the first pivot step, rows 2 and 3 are (0, 3, 5, 2) and (0, −6, −12, −4). R3 ← R3 + 2R2 gives (0, 0, −2, 0).

questions.category: LU factorization: computing L and U
questions.q: A has rows (1, 3, 4, 0), (−3, −6, −7, 2), (3, 3, 0, −4), (−5, −3, 2, 9). What is entry (4, 2) of L in its LU factorization?
questions.explain: After the first pivot step, row 4 is (0, 12, 22, 9) and column 2 from the pivot down is (3, −6, 12). Entry (4, 2) of L is 12/3 = 4 (R4 ← R4 − 4R2).

questions.category: LU factorization: computing L and U
questions.q: A has rows (1, 3, 4, 0), (−3, −6, −7, 2), (3, 3, 0, −4), (−5, −3, 2, 9). What is entry (4, 3) of L in its LU factorization?
questions.explain: After two pivot steps, rows 3 and 4 are (0, 0, −2, 0) and (0, 0, 2, 1). Column 3 from the pivot down is (−2, 2), so the multiplier is 2/(−2) = −1 (R4 ← R4 + R3).

questions.category: LU factorization: computing L and U
questions.q: What is L in an LU factorization of A with rows (1, 2, 1), (2, 7, 4), (−1, 4, 6)?
questions.explain: R2 − 2R1 gives (0, 3, 2), R3 + R1 gives (0, 6, 7), and R3 − 2R2 gives (0, 0, 3). The multipliers 2, −1, 2 fill entries (2,1), (3,1), (3,2). One wrong choice uses 6 instead of 6/3 = 2, one has every sign flipped, and one is upper triangular.

questions.category: LU factorization: computing L and U
questions.q: A has rows (2, 1, −1), (6, 1, 0), (−4, 4, 7). Find an LU factorization. What is entry (3, 2) of L?
questions.explain: R2 − 3R1 gives (0, −2, 3) and R3 + 2R1 gives (0, 6, 5). The second pivot is −2, so the multiplier for row 3 is 6/(−2) = −3 (R3 ← R3 + 3R2), which gives (0, 0, 14). L has rows (1, 0, 0), (3, 1, 0), (−2, −3, 1).

questions.category: LU factorization: computing L and U
questions.q: A has rows (2, 1, −1), (6, 1, 0), (−4, 4, 7). In its LU factorization, what is entry (3, 3) of U?
If A = LU, which procedure solves Ax = b?
choices: Solve Ly = b by forward substitution, then Ux = y by back substitution
Solve Ux = b by back substitution, then Ly = x by forward substitution
Solve Ly = b by back substitution, then Ux = y by forward substitution
Solve Lx = b and Ux = b, then add the two solutions
questions.explain: L is lower triangular, so Ly = b is solved from the top down (forward substitution). U is upper triangular, so Ux = y is solved from the bottom up (back substitution).

questions.q: If A = LU, then x solves Ax = b exactly when x solves Ux = b.
questions.explain: Ux has to equal y, the solution of Ly = b, not b itself. Solving Ux = b skips the forward-substitution step and gives the wrong answer unless L happens to be I.

questions.q: Why does solving Ly = b and then Ux = y give a solution of Ax = b?
choices: Because L and U commute, so LU = UL
Because L = I whenever A is invertible
questions.explain: Substitute A = LU and use associativity: Ax = (LU)x = L(Ux) = Ly = b.

questions.q: L is lower triangular with 1's on its diagonal. In forward substitution for Ly = b, what is y₁?
choices: y₁ is the last entry of b
y₁ cannot be found until the other entries of y are known
questions.explain: The first row of L is (1, 0, …, 0), so the first equation reads y₁ = b₁. Each later equation then uses the y's already found.
y₁ = 1. Then −3(1) + y₂ = −2 gives y₂ = 1, and 3(1) − 2(1) + y₃ = −1 gives y₃ = −2. Finishing, y₄ = 1, so y = (1, 1, −2, 1).

x₄ = 1. Then −2x₃ = −2 gives x₃ = 1, and 3x₂ + 5(1) + 2(1) = 1 gives x₂ = −2. Finishing, x₁ = 3. The solution x = (3, −2, 1, 1) checks in Ax = b for A with rows (1, 3, 4, 0), (−3, −6, −7, 2), (3, 3, 0, −4), (−5, −3, 2, 9) and b = (1, −2, −1, 2).

Forward substitution: y₁ = 2, then 2(2) + y₂ = 6 gives y₂ = 2, then −2 + 2(2) + y₃ = 5 gives y₃ = 3. Back substitution: 3x₃ = 3, then 3x₂ + 2 = 2, then x₁ + 0 + 1 = 2. So x = (1, 0, 1), and A(1, 0, 1) = (2, 6, 5) checks. (2, 2, 3) is y, not x.

questions.q: A has rows (2, 1), (6, 8), with L rows (1, 0), (3, 1) and U rows (2, 1), (0, 5). For b = (4, 22), forward-solve Ly = b. What is y₂?
questions.explain: y₁ = 4, then 3(4) + y₂ = 22 gives y₂ = 10. Shortcut check: applying R2 − 3R1 to b = (4, 22) also gives (4, 10).

questions.q: U has rows (2, 1), (0, 5) and y = (4, 10). Back-solve Ux = y. What is x₁?
questions.explain: 5x₂ = 10 gives x₂ = 2, then 2x₁ + 2 = 4 gives x₁ = 1. Check with A having rows (2, 1), (6, 8): A(1, 2) = (2 + 2, 6 + 16) = (4, 22).

questions.q: L has rows (1, 0, 0), (3, 1, 0), (−2, −3, 1) and b = (1, 8, 25). Forward-solve Ly = b. What is y₃?
questions.explain: y₁ = 1. Then 3(1) + y₂ = 8 gives y₂ = 5, and −2(1) − 3(5) + y₃ = 25 gives y₃ = 25 + 2 + 15 = 42.

questions.q: U has rows (2, 1, −1), (0, −2, 3), (0, 0, 14) and y = (1, 5, 42). Back-solve Ux = y. What is x₂?
questions.explain: 14x₃ = 42 gives x₃ = 3. Then −2x₂ + 3(3) = 5 gives x₂ = 2, and 2x₁ + 2 − 3 = 1 gives x₁ = 1. Check with A = LU, which has rows (2, 1, −1), (6, 1, 0), (−4, 4, 7): A(1, 2, 3) = (1, 8, 25).

questions.q: If A = LU, the vector y that solves Ly = b is the same vector you get by applying to b the row operations that turned A into U.
questions.explain: The row operations turn L into I and A into U. Applied to b they give a vector y with Ly = b. For example, with A having rows (2, 1), (6, 8) and b = (4, 22), the step R2 − 3R1 gives y = (4, 10).

questions.q: For A with rows (1, 3, 4, 0), (−3, −6, −7, 2), (3, 3, 0, −4), (−5, −3, 2, 9), the equation Ax = b has exactly one solution for each b in ℝ⁴.
questions.explain: The U in its LU factorization has 4 pivots, so every column of A is a pivot column and A is invertible by the IMT. Ax = b is then consistent for every b, and with no free variables the solution is unique.
